title: Or, And, Neither — on a Table

steps.body:
"Bus **or** sport" on a table means: shade the whole bus row, then shade the whole sport column. The cell where they cross gets shaded twice — once by the row, once by the column.

That is the addition rule in picture form. Add the row total and the column total, then take the crossing cell back once.
The four inner cells of the student table.

widget.prompt: Tap every cell that belongs to "takes the bus **or** plays a sport".

hotspots.label: walks, no sport: 30
hotspots.feedback: These 30 walk and play no sport, so they satisfy neither event. They are the only cell outside the union.

widget.missFeedback: A cell belongs if it is in the bus ROW or in the sport COLUMN — one condition is enough.
widget.successFeedback: Three cells: 40 + 60 + 70 = 170 students. The fourth cell, 30, is the "neither" group.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents table union.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for table union must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines table union.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

predict.prompt: On the table, "takes the bus OR plays a sport" means shading…

options.label: The whole bus row and the whole sport column
Only the cell where the row and the column cross

predict.reveal: The whole row and the whole column. The crossing cell is the students who do both — it belongs to "or" and gets shaded, but only once. Shading only the crossing is "and", which is a different and much smaller group of students.

explanationVariants: Count the shaded cells directly: 40 + 60 + 70 = 170, and 170/200 = 0.85. The rule and the cells agree, as they must.

widget.prompt: P(takes the bus **or** plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 0.50 + 0.55 with nothing subtracted — and a probability above 1 is the tell. The 40 in the crossing cell got counted twice.
That is the joint cell, P(bus and sport). "Or" is the larger event: it also holds for the 60 bus riders with no sport and the 70 walkers who play.
That is P(sport) alone. The 60 bus riders who play no sport still satisfy "bus or sport".

widget.fallbackFeedback: 0.50 + 0.55 − 0.20 = 0.85, which matches the 170 shaded students out of 200.

steps.body: Say why the subtraction is there.
explanationVariants: The bus row already contains the 40 bus riders who play a sport, and the sport column contains them again. Adding row and column counts them twice, so remove one copy.
170 students are shaded, but 100 + 110 = 210. The 40-cell explains the whole 40-student gap.

widget.prompt: Why do we subtract the 40 when we add the bus row (100) to the sport column (110)?

options.label: Those 40 students sit in both the row and the column, so they are counted twice.
options.feedback: Exactly — 100 + 110 = 210, which overshoots the 170 shaded students by precisely those 40.

options.label: Because those 40 students belong to neither event.
options.feedback: The 40 belong to BOTH events, which is why they are double-counted. The students who belong to neither are the 30 in the last cell.

options.label: To make the probability come out under 1.
options.feedback: Staying under 1 is a symptom, not the reason. The subtraction exists because a double-counted student must be counted once.

options.label: Because the row and the column have different totals.
options.feedback: Unequal totals are fine — the row and column here happen to be 100 and 110. The correction is about the shared cell, not the sizes.

steps.body:
"**Neither**" is the complement of "or". Every student is either inside the shaded union or outside it, so:

P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).

On a table it is the one cell you never shaded. That gives you a free check: the union and the "neither" cell must add to the whole group.

explanationVariants: 1 − 0.85 = 0.15, and the unshaded cell holds 30 students: 30/200 = 0.15. Same answer, two routes.
Only the walkers with no sport miss both events. There are 30 of them, out of 200.

widget.prompt: P(neither takes the bus nor plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the union itself — the students who DO satisfy at least one event. "Neither" is what is left over: 1 − 0.85.
That is P(walks). Walking alone is not enough — the 70 walkers who play a sport still satisfy the "sport" half.
That is P(no sport), the whole column. The 60 bus riders inside it are still in the union via the bus row.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The single unshaded cell holds 30 students: 30/200 = 0.15 = 1 − 0.85.

explanationVariants: "At least one" is the union, so its complement is "neither" — the single cell that satisfies no condition.
Any "at least one" question can be answered by finding the one way to fail and subtracting from 1.

widget.prompt: A student is picked at random. Which pair of events are complements?

options.label: "Bus or sport" and "walks and no sport"
options.feedback: Right — they cover the table with no overlap, so their probabilities must sum to 1: 0.85 + 0.15.

options.label: "Bus or sport" and "bus and sport"
options.feedback: These overlap heavily — the 40 in the crossing cell satisfy both descriptions. Complements can share no one.

options.label: "Takes the bus" and "plays a sport"
options.feedback: A student can do both (40 do) and a student can do neither (30 do). Complements allow neither case.

options.label: "Walks" and "plays no sport"
options.feedback: These two overlap in the 30 walkers with no sport, so they are not complements. Their probabilities sum to 0.95, not 1.

hints: First find how many phones have at least one of the two — that is the union.
Union = 90 + 60 − 40 = 110 phones have a case or a protector (or both).
"Neither" is everyone else: 150 − 110 = 40. Divide by 150 and round to three places.
explanationVariants: Build the four cells: both 40, case-only 50, protector-only 20, and the rest neither: 150 − 40 − 50 − 20 = 40 → 0.267.

widget.prompt: Of 150 phones, 90 have a case, 60 have a screen protector, and 40 have both. Find **P(neither)** as a decimal, rounded to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the union, 110/150 — the phones with at least one accessory. "Neither" is the leftover: 1 − 0.733.
That is 80/150, which comes from subtracting the 40 overlap twice. It is added twice by 90 + 60, so it comes off exactly once.
That comes from 90 + 60 = 150, as if every phone had exactly one accessory. But 40 phones have both, so those two counts overlap and the union is only 110.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 90 + 60 − 40 = 110 phones have at least one, so 150 − 110 = 40 have neither: 40/150 ≈ 0.267.

takeaways: "Or" on a table = a row plus a column, minus the cell where they cross.
"Neither" is the complement of "or": P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) — the cell you never shaded.
The rule and the raw cell counts must agree; disagreement means the overlap was mishandled.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: someone tells you the student takes the bus. The denominator changes.

concept.body: Use the same 200-student table: 100 take the bus, 110 play a sport, and 40 do both. `100 + 110 − 40 = 170` shades exactly the students in the bus row or sport column. That is `170/200 = 0.85`; if an "or" probability exceeds 1, the crossing cell was not subtracted once.

explanationVariants: 100 + 110 = 210, but only 170 students are shaded. The gap is 40 — the crossing cell, counted twice.
210 − 170 = 40, which is exactly the bus-and-sport cell.

widget.prompt: The bus row totals 100 and the sport column totals 110. By how many students does 100 + 110 overshoot the 170 who are in the union?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the union itself. The overshoot is the difference: 210 − 170.
That is the "neither" cell, which sits outside the union entirely. The overshoot comes from the cell inside BOTH events.
